quiz.question: Which statement correctly describes TCP?
options: It preserves application message boundaries
It is a connection-oriented byte stream
It guarantees every application request is processed
It has no flow control
quiz.explanation: TCP provides an unstructured, connection-oriented byte stream with sequence tracking and flow control. It does NOT preserve application message boundaries (framing is the responsibility of the application protocol).

quiz.question: What is a major advantage of epoll for Linux servers?
options: It eliminates all network latency
It can efficiently monitor readiness across many descriptors
It automatically makes all application code non-blocking
It guarantees zero packet loss
quiz.explanation: epoll maintains an in-kernel interest list (red-black tree) and only returns descriptors that are currently ready (O(1) retrieval), avoiding the expensive O(N) scanning of select() and poll() when thousands of sockets are mostly idle.

quiz.question: What does application backpressure accomplish?
options: Makes the NIC transmit at unlimited speed
Prevents the application from accepting work indefinitely beyond its capacity
Disables TCP congestion control
Guarantees requests finish immediately
quiz.explanation: Application backpressure signals the upstream sender or pauses socket reads when downstream processing queues are full, preventing unconstrained memory growth, queue bloat, and catastrophic service collapse.

quiz.question: Which architecture is often useful for many mostly idle connections?
options: One operating-system process per byte
An event loop using non-blocking sockets
An unbounded number of threads
A busy loop repeatedly polling every socket
quiz.explanation: A single-threaded or small multi-reactor event loop with non-blocking sockets and epoll multiplexes tens of thousands of idle connections with negligible memory overhead (no dedicated per-connection thread stacks).

quiz.question: What does a Linux network namespace isolate?
options: Every hardware device on the entire machine
A network view including interfaces and routes
All memory shared by all processes
The CPU instruction set
quiz.explanation: A Linux network namespace provides an isolated networking stack, including its own network interfaces, routing tables, port binding allocation tables, and firewall rules.

quiz.question: Why measure p95 latency as well as throughput?
options: p95 measures RAM capacity
Throughput alone reveals all slow requests
Tail latency shows how slower requests behave under load
p95 always equals average latency
quiz.explanation: Throughput and average latency conceal queueing delays and tail spikes. High-percentile latency (p95 and p99) reflects the experience of outlier requests that suffer from socket buffer queue bloat, context switching, and worker starvation.

theorySections.title: Network Interfaces and the Linux Kernel Networking Path
paragraphs: When an application sends or receives data over a network socket, it does not manipulate raw Ethernet frames or cable electrical pulses directly. It relies on the operating system’s socket abstraction and layered network subsystem to coordinate protocol state, buffer allocations, hardware queueing, and DMA transfers.
Step through each kernel layer and inspect memory structures during packet transmission or reception.
A network interface represents a logical or physical endpoint through which the Linux kernel transmits and receives packets.

theorySections.title: Sockets, TCP/UDP APIs, and Connection Lifecycle
paragraphs: In Linux, a socket is represented by an integer file descriptor in the process's file descriptor table. This allows standard POSIX operations such as read(), write(), poll(), and close().
Why recv() does not preserve boundaries: a stream can deliver partial fragments or coalesce multiple writes into one chunk.

theorySections.title: Blocking, Non-Blocking, and Multiplexed I/O
paragraphs: The central challenge in network server engineering is answering: What should a thread do while a network socket has no incoming data ready? The choice between blocking execution, non-blocking polling, and event multiplexing dictates maximum concurrency and system resource consumption.
Calls to recv() put the calling thread to sleep (TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE) until data arrives, timeout expires, or peer closes.
Set via fcntl(O_NONBLOCK). Syscall returns immediately with EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK if not ready.
One single thread asks the kernel: "Wake me up only when ANY of these 50,000 sockets becomes readable or writable."

theorySections.title: select, poll, epoll, and Event-Driven Servers
paragraphs: As the internet transitioned from serving hundreds of connections to millions of persistent WebSockets and HTTP/2 streams (the classic C10K and C1000K problem), the limitations of early Unix polling primitives led Linux kernel engineers to build epoll.
Vary the total number of monitored connections and active sockets to observe kernel complexity scaling.

{triggerMode === "LT" ? "epoll_wait() continues returning the file descriptor on every call as long as unread bytes remain in the socket receive buffer." : "epoll_wait() triggers only on the state transition from not-ready to ready. The application MUST loop non-blocking recv() until EAGAIN."}
Standard library selectors.DefaultSelector() automatically binds to Linux epoll.

theorySections.title: Socket Buffers, Queues, and Backpressure
paragraphs: Networking is not merely sending bytes; every stage in the kernel, device driver, and user-space application has finite queues. When the sender produces data faster than the receiver consumes it, unconstrained queues will grow until the system exhausts memory or suffers crippling tail latency spikes.
Observe how client transmission rates and server consumption rates trigger TCP zero-window probing and application backpressure.

theorySections.title: Network Namespaces and Local Isolation
paragraphs: A Linux network namespace provides a completely isolated virtual copy of the networking stack. Container runtimes (such as Docker, Podman, and Kubernetes CRI-O) use network namespaces to guarantee that container applications have their own interfaces, routing tables, and port allocations without conflicting with the host system.
Create two network namespaces and link them through a virtual Ethernet wire (veth pair).

theorySections.title: How Servers Scale Across Processes, Threads, and Event Loops
paragraphs: There is no single "best" server architecture for all workloads. The optimal design depends on concurrent connection counts, ratio of CPU computation to I/O wait, memory limits, and latency targets.
Compare Process-per-connection, Thread-per-connection, Thread Pool, and Event Loop under increasing client load.

theorySections.title: Build and Benchmark a Concurrent TCP Server
paragraphs: Implement a bounded multi-threaded TCP server, generate concurrent client load, and measure how throughput and p95 tail latency change across 1, 5, 10, 25, and 50 concurrency levels.
Bounded multi-threaded server with semaphore connection slots and socket timeout.

{`# threaded_server.py import socket import threading from socketserver import ThreadingMixIn, TCPServer, StreamRequestHandler HOST = "127.0.0.1" PORT = 9000 MAX_CONNECTIONS = 100 class EchoHandler(StreamRequestHandler): timeout = 3 def handle(self): while True: try: line = self.rfile.readline() if not line: break self.wfile.write(line) self.wfile.flush() except (socket.timeout, ConnectionResetError, BrokenPipeError): break class BoundedThreadingServer(ThreadingMixIn, TCPServer): daemon_threads = True allow_reuse_address = True request_queue_size = 128 def __init__(self, address, handler): self.connection_slots = threading.BoundedSemaphore(MAX_CONNECTIONS) super().__init__(address, handler) def process_request(self, request, client_address): if not self.connection_slots.acquire(blocking=False): request.close() return try: super().process_request(request, client_address) except Exception: self.connection_slots.release() raise def process_request_thread(self, request, client_address): try: super().process_request_thread(request, client_address) finally: self.connection_slots.release() if __name__ == "__main__": print(f"[*] Bounded TCP server listening on {HOST}:{PORT}") with BoundedThreadingServer((HOST, PORT), EchoHandler) as server: try: server.serve_forever() except KeyboardInterrupt: print("\\n[*] Shutting down server gracefully.")`} {/* Step 2: Benchmark Client Script */} Step 2 — Save bench_client.py Multi-threaded benchmark load generator measuring completed requests, throughput, and p95 latency.

{`# bench_client.py import argparse, socket, statistics, time from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed def worker(host, port, requests): latencies = [] errors = 0 try: with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=3) as sock: sock.settimeout(3) reader = sock.makefile("rb") for _ in range(requests): msg = b"hello\\n" t0 = time.perf_counter() try: sock.sendall(msg) resp = reader.readline() if resp != msg: errors += 1 continue latencies.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000) except (OSError, TimeoutError): errors += 1 except (OSError, TimeoutError): errors += requests return latencies, errors`} {/* Step 3: Concurrency Execution Table */} Step 3 — Run Increasing Concurrency Tests Concurrency Test Command Completed Throughput (req/s) p95 Latency Errors {[1, 5, 10, 25, 50].map((c) => ( {c} clients python3 bench_client.py --concurrency {c} --requests 100 Measure Measure Measure Measure ))} {/* Step 4: Monitoring Commands */} Step 4 — Live Monitoring Commands (Terminal 3) $ top -H -p $(pgrep -f threaded_server) Shows thread count, per-thread CPU utilization, and state.
Monitors active connected sockets and socket queue depth.
Monitors system context switches (cs) and runnable queue (r).
